messages.content: I want to investigate contact-rich insertion policies that can distinguish recoverable misalignment from jamming under visual occlusion and unknown friction.

The distinction is central to the goal: a policy should not treat every difficult contact as a jam, or treat a jam as merely an alignment error it can keep pushing through. Visual occlusion limits what can be inferred from sight, while unknown friction makes contact behavior harder to interpret. This is an investigation objective, not a claim that a policy already makes the distinction reliably.
What would count as success for the insertion part?

The stated target is at least 90% insertion success on held-out peg geometries and friction conditions, with 0.2 mm clearance. “Held-out” matters: the target concerns conditions beyond those used to develop the policy, not just familiar examples. The goal does not specify a particular peg shape or how the friction conditions are distributed.
And the force limit is separate from insertion success?

Yes. Peak contact force must stay below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including trials involving jam recovery. A high insertion-success rate would not, by itself, establish that the force target was met; likewise, meeting the force target alone would not establish the required insertion-success rate.
Why emphasize peak force rather than just saying contact should be gentle?

“Peak” makes the constraint about the highest contact force reached in a trial, not merely its typical or average force. “Below 20 N” is also a strict threshold: a peak of exactly 20 N would not be below it. The requirement applies to at least 99% of trials, rather than asserting that no trial can ever exceed the limit.
Does including jam recovery mean we can set aside those trials when checking force?

No. Jam recovery is explicitly included in the force requirement. The stated target is not a separate 99% guarantee for the subset of jam-recovery trials, but those trials are not excluded from the trials considered for the peak-force criterion.
How should I understand the difference between a recoverable misalignment and jamming here?

At the level of this goal, recoverable misalignment is an insertion difficulty from which the policy may still make progress, whereas jamming is the condition it must recognize as distinct rather than simply continuing as though the alignment issue were recoverable. The node does not prescribe an operational test for either label. Investigating how to make that distinction under uncertain observations is part of the work.
So the aim isn't just to identify a jam after insertion has already failed?

Right. The goal concerns insertion policies: the distinction needs to be useful in how the policy handles contact, including potential jam recovery. It does not specify when a classification must occur or prescribe a particular recovery maneuver. The stated performance targets still apply to the policy's trials.
Does visual occlusion mean the policy cannot use vision at all?

Not necessarily. “Under visual occlusion” says visual information is obstructed; it does not say that vision is wholly unavailable or define the extent of the obstruction. The important point is that the distinction between recoverable misalignment and jamming cannot be framed as though an unobstructed view were guaranteed.
And does unknown friction mean we assume one especially difficult friction value?

No particular value is given. The goal is to investigate the policy under unknown friction and to reach the insertion-success target on held-out friction conditions, alongside held-out peg geometries. It does not name a friction coefficient, range, or single worst-case condition.
With 0.2 mm clearance, should we describe the target as applying to some looser fit as well?

The specified clearance is 0.2 mm. We can describe the target at that clearance, but should not silently extend the numerical requirement to other clearances or assume how the clearance is defined beyond what is stated.
Suppose a policy reaches 90% success but has a few unusually forceful recoveries. Would its success rate settle the question?

No. At least 90% insertion success is one requirement, and keeping peak contact force below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including jam recovery, is another. The forceful recoveries would need to be assessed against the peak-force criterion; insertion success does not waive it. That hypothetical alone does not establish whether the force requirement is met.
Conversely, could a policy satisfy the force target by avoiding contact and rarely inserting?

Keeping force low would not be enough. The policy also needs at least 90% insertion success on the specified held-out peg geometries and friction conditions with 0.2 mm clearance. The two thresholds are meant to be read together, without reducing one to the other.
Is there a required sensing method or particular way to recover from a jam?

Neither is specified here. The objective identifies the distinction the policy should make, the challenging conditions—visual occlusion and unknown friction—and the insertion and peak-force targets. It leaves open how a policy infers its contact state and how it handles a jam.
I don't want the wording to imply that unknown friction and occlusion have already been solved.

Then keep the wording prospective: investigate policies that distinguish recoverable misalignment from jamming under those conditions, aiming for the stated success and force thresholds. No results are supplied, so neither the distinction nor either performance target should be presented as already achieved.
Can you state the objective in one precise sentence without losing the two numerical requirements?

Investigate contact-rich insertion policies that distinguish recoverable misalignment from jamming under visual occlusion and unknown friction, aiming for at least 90% insertion success on held-out peg geometries and friction conditions with 0.2 mm clearance while keeping peak contact force below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including jam recovery.
What approach would you propose for making that distinction when the insertion is visually occluded?

Use geometry-conditioned, friction-adaptive beliefs based on wrench history to distinguish recoverable misalignment from jamming under occlusion. The policy would use that belief to select either probing capped at 18 N or retreat. This is a proposed approach, not a result showing that it works.
What does “wrench-history belief” mean in this proposal?

A wrench describes force and torque. A wrench-history belief is an estimate of the contact situation informed by how those quantities have behaved over time, rather than by a single reading. Calling it a belief also leaves room for uncertainty: the policy is estimating whether the contact is more consistent with misalignment or jamming, not directly observing an infallible label.
Why condition that belief on geometry?

The interpretation of contact can depend on the peg geometry. Geometry-conditioned means the belief takes geometry into account when interpreting the wrench history, rather than assuming the same history has the same meaning for every geometry. The proposal does not specify a geometry representation or claim that conditioning alone will meet the held-out-geometry success target.
And what is meant by friction-adaptive if friction is unknown?

It means the interpretation should be able to adjust to friction conditions rather than relying on a friction value known in advance. That matters because unknown friction can complicate the interpretation of contact during insertion. The proposal does not specify how the adjustment is implemented or imply that the friction value has already been identified.
Is the policy supposed to decide with certainty whether it is misaligned or jammed?

No certainty is specified. The proposed belief supports a distinction between recoverable misalignment and jamming despite occlusion and unknown friction. Describing it as a belief avoids pretending that an uncertain contact state is directly visible or that every case will be unambiguous.
What actions does that distinction lead to?

The proposed choice is between 18 N-capped probing and retreat. Probing is the bounded contact action in the proposal; retreat is the alternative when continuing to probe is not the selected response. The proposal does not specify an exact decision threshold, a probing motion, or a retreat trajectory.
Does the 18 N cap apply to both options?

The wording specifically describes probing as 18 N-capped. It does not state a separate numerical cap for retreat. Retreat still falls within the overall goal's trial-level peak-contact-force requirement; that requirement includes jam recovery.
How does that 18 N number relate to the goal of keeping peak contact force below 20 N?

They serve different roles. The proposal calls for 18 N-capped probing, while the goal requires peak contact force below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including jam recovery. Proposing an 18 N cap for probing does not, by itself, establish that measured trial peaks will stay below 20 N, particularly when the goal covers the entire trial rather than only probing.
Should we describe retreat as proof that a jam has been detected?

No. Retreat is one of the actions selected using the belief; choosing it need not be described as proof of an underlying state. The proposal is about distinguishing misalignment from jamming well enough to inform that choice under uncertainty, not about obtaining a certain diagnosis.
Could probing be described as always the right response to recoverable misalignment?

That would be stronger than the proposal states. It links the belief about misalignment or jamming to a choice between capped probing and retreat, but it does not give a rule that every recoverable misalignment must prompt probing. Nor does it say that every probe will resolve the misalignment.
Is there a specified model architecture behind these beliefs?

No architecture is specified. “Geometry-conditioned,” “friction-adaptive,” and “wrench-history” describe information and capabilities the proposed belief should use. They do not commit the investigation to a particular estimator, training procedure, or contact-state classifier.
Does relying on wrench history mean vision is ruled out?

The proposal says to use wrench-history beliefs under occlusion. It does not assert that all visual information is unavailable or impose a general ban on vision. Its point is that the distinction should not depend on an unobstructed visual view of the contact.
How does this proposal connect to the held-out insertion target without claiming it has been met?

It proposes a way to make contact-state decisions that could be investigated against that target: at least 90% insertion success on held-out peg geometries and friction conditions with 0.2 mm clearance. Geometry conditioning and friction adaptation are relevant to those varying conditions, but their inclusion is not evidence that the success rate has been achieved.
Could I say the 18 N cap replaces the 20 N requirement?

No. The 18 N cap is part of the proposed probing action. The requirement remains peak contact force below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including jam recovery. Both values should be retained with their distinct scopes.
Give me a compact formulation of the proposal.

Use geometry-conditioned, friction-adaptive beliefs from wrench history to distinguish recoverable misalignment from jamming under visual occlusion, then select either 18 N-capped probing or retreat. This is a proposed policy approach to investigate, not a claim that the insertion-success or peak-force targets have been achieved.
Can 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped lateral probes distinguish recoverable offsets from wedging by wrench history under occlusion and unknown friction?

That is the question to investigate, not an established result. The proposed distinction would come from how force and torque evolve during the 0.1 mm lateral probes, while keeping those probes capped at 18 N. The challenge is whether that history remains informative when the contact is visually occluded and friction is unknown.
What exactly is being distinguished?

The two possibilities are a recoverable offset and wedging. A recoverable offset is a misalignment from which insertion can still be recovered; wedging is the contrasting contact condition the probe is meant to identify rather than mistake for a recoverable offset. The question does not supply a definitive wrench pattern for either one.
Does “by wrench history” mean the policy should use more than the force at the end of a probe?

Yes. A wrench includes force and torque, and its history is their behavior over time. The question asks whether that history during probing can support the distinction; it does not specify which part of the history is decisive or rule out uncertainty after the probe.
Why specify a lateral probe?

“Lateral” identifies the direction of the proposed probing motion as sideways rather than simply continuing insertion. The question is specifically about whether the resulting wrench history can distinguish the two conditions. It does not prescribe a particular lateral direction, a motion sequence, or a rule for interpreting the response.
Is 0.1 mm the offset we are trying to detect?

No. In this question, 0.1 mm describes the lateral probe, not the size of a recoverable offset. No offset magnitude is specified, so the question should not be narrowed to detecting offsets of exactly 0.1 mm.
And the 18 N figure describes the probe rather than a measured outcome?
Correct. The probe is described as 18 N-capped. That is a constraint on the proposed probing action, not a report that a probe was performed or that any measured peak stayed within the cap.
If the probe is force-capped, does that guarantee it will reveal whether the contact is wedged?

No. The cap limits the proposed probing action; it does not establish how informative the resulting wrench history will be. The central uncertainty is whether useful separation between recoverable offsets and wedging is possible within a 0.1 mm lateral probe capped at 18 N.
Could the same wrench history be consistent with both possibilities?

That possibility is part of why the question remains open. Under occlusion and unknown friction, a wrench history might not uniquely identify the contact condition. The question asks whether the histories are sufficiently distinguishable for the intended distinction, not whether every individual history must have an unambiguous interpretation.
What does occlusion change about how we read the question?

It means the distinction is being asked for when the contact cannot be assumed to be plainly visible. The proposed evidence is wrench history from the lateral probes. The question does not specify how much of the scene is occluded or say that all visual information is absent.
Does unknown friction make this a question about estimating a friction coefficient?

Not specifically. Friction is unknown in the conditions under which the distinction must be investigated. The question does not require a numerical friction estimate, and it does not state that friction must be identified before wrench history can be interpreted.
Could we answer yes just because recoverable offsets and wedging have different meanings?

No. They are different conditions by definition, but that does not show that 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped lateral probes produce wrench histories that distinguish them under occlusion and unknown friction. Whether the proposed observations support that distinction is precisely what is being asked.
Would one wrench reading count as answering the question?

A single reading would not, by itself, address the emphasis on wrench history. More importantly, the question is about whether the history supports distinguishing the two contact conditions under the stated uncertainties. It does not specify a minimum number of readings, probes, or trials.
Does the plural “probes” commit us to a particular number or pattern of lateral motions?

No particular number or pattern is given. The specified features are that the probes are lateral, 0.1 mm, and 18 N-capped. Adding a particular sequence or directional pattern would go beyond this question.
Should we expect a particular torque sign or force trend to identify wedging?

The question does not state such a signature. Force and torque history are the proposed basis for distinguishing the conditions, but assigning a particular sign, trend, or cutoff to wedging would be an additional hypothesis, not something established here.
How does this relate to the earlier idea of a belief about contact state?

The probe question focuses on whether wrench history generated by a specified, bounded lateral motion is informative about recoverable offsets versus wedging. That information could be relevant to a belief about contact state, but the question itself does not specify a belief update or a decision rule.
Is it fair to call this a safety question as well as an information question?

It has both aspects: it asks whether the probe is informative, and it explicitly caps the proposed probe at 18 N. The cap alone is not a demonstrated safety result, however. It should not be confused with a measured peak-contact-force outcome for an entire insertion trial.
Would a probe that gives no clear distinction necessarily show the whole insertion approach cannot work?

No. It would bear on the question of whether these particular 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped lateral probes distinguish recoverable offsets from wedging by wrench history under the stated conditions. The question does not authorize a broader conclusion about every possible insertion policy or probing action.
And if those histories did distinguish the two conditions, would that alone establish insertion success?

No. An informative distinction would answer this probing question, but it would not by itself establish how often insertion succeeds or what peak contact force occurs across full trials. Those are broader performance matters, separate from whether the specified probes provide useful wrench-history evidence.
Can you phrase the question so the limits on what we know remain explicit?

Can wrench histories from 0.1 mm lateral probes capped at 18 N distinguish recoverable offsets from wedging when contact is visually occluded and friction is unknown? That wording keeps the proposed motion, force cap, evidence, and two conditions explicit without assuming that the distinction has already been demonstrated.
I want to make a testable hypothesis out of the probe question. What should it say?

Hypothesis: under occlusion, wrench histories from 0.1 mm probes capped at 18 N achieve jam-versus-offset AUROC of at least 0.90 across unseen geometries and friction conditions. This predicts discrimination performance; it does not report a measured result.
What does the AUROC target mean here?

AUROC summarizes how well a score separates jam cases from offset cases across possible decision thresholds. An AUROC of at least 0.90 would indicate strong ranking discrimination by the wrench-history evidence. It does not mean that at least 90% of individual cases are classified correctly at a particular threshold.
So exactly 0.90 would satisfy the hypothesis?
Yes. The target is ≥0.90, so 0.90 meets it; a value below 0.90 does not. The hypothesis does not specify a particular operating threshold for turning scores into jam-or-offset decisions.
Are we hypothesizing 90% insertion success, too?

Not in this statement. The predicted outcome here is jam-versus-offset AUROC ≥0.90 from wrench histories under the stated conditions. Distinguishing those conditions could matter to an insertion policy, but discrimination performance is not the same measure as insertion success.
What precisely supplies the evidence for the distinction?

Wrench histories from the 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped probes. “Wrench” refers to force and torque, and “history” emphasizes their behavior during probing rather than a single force reading. The hypothesis does not identify a particular feature of that history as the decisive one.
Does 0.1 mm describe the offset we're trying to classify?
No. It specifies the probe size in the hypothesis, not the magnitude of an offset. No size range for the offset cases is given.
The probe question described lateral probes. Is that still the context?

Yes, this hypothesis addresses that probe question. Its own stated prediction concerns wrench histories from 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped probes and their jam-versus-offset AUROC. It does not add a particular lateral direction, probe sequence, or motion-control method.
Does the 18 N cap mean the hypothesis also predicts that peak contact force stays below 18 N throughout insertion?

No. The 18 N cap describes the probes. The hypothesis does not predict a measured peak for an entire insertion trial, including any actions outside probing, and it does not establish a trial-level force guarantee.
Why explicitly say “under occlusion” rather than treating that as background?

Because occlusion is a condition of the prediction. The proposed discrimination is meant to hold without assuming an unobstructed view of the contact. The hypothesis does not define the extent of occlusion or claim that all visual information is absent.
How strong is the claim about geometry and friction?

It predicts AUROC ≥0.90 across unseen geometries and friction conditions, rather than only for familiar ones. It does not list those geometries or friction conditions, define a friction range, or state that the target must be met separately in every individual condition.
Could we say it predicts AUROC ≥0.90 for every unseen geometry–friction pairing?

That would add a stronger, per-pairing guarantee not stated in the hypothesis. “Across unseen geometries and friction” preserves the intended generalization claim without specifying how results are broken down by pairing.
Unknown friction was part of the original probe question. Does this hypothesis require knowing friction before interpreting the wrench history?

No such requirement is stated. The hypothesis places the discrimination claim across unseen friction conditions, consistent with the question's unknown-friction setting. It does not specify whether friction is estimated, represented implicitly, or handled in some other way.
Does “jam-versus-offset” give us an exact labeling rule?

No. It identifies the two classes whose discrimination AUROC is predicted. The hypothesis does not provide an operational rule for labeling an observation as a jam or an offset, nor does it name a particular score or classifier.
Could a high AUROC still leave some individual cases ambiguous?

Yes. AUROC is a summary of discrimination across cases and thresholds; even an AUROC at or above 0.90 would not mean every jam and offset is unambiguously distinguished. The hypothesis sets a performance target, not a promise of perfect identification.
Should I describe the wrench response of a jam as always increasing during a probe?

Not on the basis of this hypothesis. It predicts a level of jam-versus-offset discrimination from wrench histories but specifies no universal force or torque pattern for either class. Adding one would be a separate claim.
Does reaching the AUROC target tell us which action to take after probing?
Not by itself. AUROC concerns discrimination over possible thresholds. The hypothesis does not choose a decision threshold or specify when to probe again, continue, or retreat in an individual case.
Can we present the ≥0.90 figure as an observed result now?

No. It is the numerical prediction in a hypothesis. No observations or evaluation results are supplied here, so it should remain phrased as a target to test rather than a performance already achieved.
Please give me a concise version that keeps that distinction clear.

We hypothesize that, under occlusion, wrench histories from 0.1 mm probes capped at 18 N will distinguish jams from offsets with AUROC ≥0.90 across unseen geometries and friction conditions. The AUROC value is predicted, not observed.
How would we plan to investigate whether the occluded probes distinguish jams from offsets?

Collect wrench traces from probes under occlusion across friction and geometry splits, label the cases as jams or offsets, and evaluate classifier AUROC and peak force. That is a plan for gathering and assessing evidence, not a report that the traces have been collected or that the distinction works.
What counts as a wrench trace in that plan?

It is a record of force and torque over the course of a probe. Keeping the history matters because the question is whether the evolving contact response, rather than just one reading, helps distinguish jams from offsets. The plan does not prescribe a recording rate or a particular way to turn the trace into classifier input.
Are these the 0.1 mm lateral probes capped at 18 N that we were discussing?

Yes, those are the probes this plan is meant to investigate. The plan calls for collecting their occluded wrench traces and assessing both discrimination and peak force. It does not add a particular lateral direction or sequence of motions.
What does “across friction and geometry splits” add?

It makes variation in friction and geometry part of the planned collection and evaluation, rather than examining only one combination. The plan does not state which geometries or friction conditions to include, how many there are, or the precise assignment of cases to splits.
Should we specify that the classifier knows the friction value for each probe?

That is not specified. Collecting traces across friction splits does not mean the classifier is given a known friction value for each case. The plan leaves open what information the classifier receives beyond the wrench traces.
Why do we need jam-versus-offset labels if we're evaluating AUROC?

AUROC assesses how well classifier scores separate the two labeled classes, so the evaluation needs to identify which collected cases are jams and which are offsets. The plan calls for those labels but does not provide an operational labeling procedure or a claim that labeling is already complete.
Is an offset label meant to cover every possible insertion difficulty that isn't a jam?

The stated contrast is jams versus offsets, in the context of recoverable offsets and wedging. The plan does not define a broader taxonomy of insertion difficulties, so it would be too much to say that every other difficulty must receive an offset label.
What would classifier AUROC tell us once we have the traces and labels?

It would summarize how well the classifier ranks jam cases against offset cases across decision thresholds. That addresses whether the recorded wrench histories contain usable evidence for this distinction. AUROC alone would not select an action threshold or show that every individual case is classified correctly.
Does the plan commit us to a particular classifier?
No. It says to evaluate classifier AUROC, but names no architecture, training method, input representation, or decision rule. Those details should not be presented as already decided.
Why evaluate peak force as well as AUROC?

The two measures answer different questions. AUROC concerns jam-versus-offset discrimination; peak force records the highest contact force reached in the evaluated probing context. A trace could be informative without, on that basis alone, establishing that the force behavior meets the intended constraint. The plan calls for measuring both rather than inferring one from the other.
Does measuring peak force mean the probes have already stayed under their 18 N cap?

No. The 18 N cap describes the proposed probes; evaluating peak force is how their observed force behavior can be assessed. No measurements are reported in this plan, so it cannot claim that any observed peak has stayed below 18 N.
Can classifier AUROC or probe peak force alone establish the full insertion-policy targets?

No. This plan evaluates classification from occluded probe traces and peak force. It does not, by itself, measure insertion success across full trials or establish the goal of peak contact force below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including jam recovery. Those trial-level claims should not be inferred from this planned probe evaluation.
Do the geometry and friction splits guarantee the classifier will work on every unseen condition?

No. Splits provide a way to examine performance across differing conditions; they are not a guarantee of performance in every condition. The plan does not specify a per-condition criterion or report results from any split.
Should we describe the data as already collected, since the plan says to collect it?
No. “Collect” is a planned action here. The same applies to labeling and evaluation: the plan states what to do, not what has been completed or observed.
Can you put the plan into one sentence without slipping in extra design choices?
Collect wrench traces from the 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped lateral probes under occlusion across friction and geometry splits, label jams versus offsets, and evaluate classifier AUROC and peak force.
Let's make the probe evaluation a concrete activity. What are we running?

Run OccludedProbe-0.2: collect labeled wrench traces from occluded 0.1 mm probes capped at 18 N, then score jam-offset AUROC and peak force on held-out geometries and friction conditions. This names the activity and what it is meant to measure; it does not report that the run has happened.
Does the “0.2” in OccludedProbe-0.2 specify another probe distance?

No additional probe distance is specified by the activity name. The probe distance stated for this run is 0.1 mm. OccludedProbe-0.2 should be retained as the activity's name without treating its suffix as a separate measurement.
What exactly do we collect during the run?

Labeled wrench traces from the occluded probes. Each trace records force and torque over the probe, and each case needs a jam or offset label for the discrimination evaluation. The activity does not specify a sampling rate, a trace representation, or a labeling procedure.
Does the 18 N cap describe the traces after collection?

It describes the probes to be run, not an observed property of traces that have already been collected. Scoring peak force is still necessary to assess what forces occurred. We should not turn the cap into a reported measurement.
Are we looking at the wrench history or only the maximum force?

Both have roles, but they answer different questions. The collected wrench traces provide histories for evaluating jam-versus-offset discrimination through AUROC. Peak force is also scored as a force outcome. Reducing the traces to their maximum force alone would not express the stated wrench-history evaluation.
Where do the held-out conditions enter?

Jam-offset AUROC and peak force are to be scored on held-out geometries and friction conditions. “Held-out” indicates that the assessment concerns conditions set aside from those used to develop the evaluated classifier or approach. The activity does not specify the split sizes, particular geometries, or friction values.
Does it require a result for each individual geometry and friction value?

It calls for scoring on held-out geometries and frictions, but does not prescribe a separate reported score for every geometry, every friction condition, or every pairing. Those would be additional reporting choices, not details already specified for OccludedProbe-0.2.
Why keep the jam and offset labels explicit?

They identify the distinction that AUROC is meant to assess. Without knowing which evaluated traces correspond to jams and which to offsets, a jam-offset AUROC would not be interpretable. The activity names the labels but leaves their operational assignment unspecified.
Can we call an offset any trace that doesn't look like a jam?

The activity does not define labels that way. It calls for labeled jam and offset cases, rather than instructing us to label a case by the very trace pattern being evaluated. No broader rule for labeling other contact situations is supplied.
What will the AUROC score tell us?

It will assess how well the evaluated scores distinguish labeled jams from labeled offsets across decision thresholds on the held-out conditions. It is a discrimination measure, not an insertion-success rate or a guarantee that every individual case receives the right action.
Is the aim to check the proposed AUROC ≥0.90 hypothesis?

Yes. Scoring jam-offset AUROC on held-out geometries and frictions provides a way to evaluate the proposed ≥0.90 discrimination target under occlusion. The activity supplies no AUROC value yet, so it does not establish whether that target is reached.
Does the activity specify the classifier we should score?

No. It says to score jam-offset AUROC, but does not name a classifier, its inputs beyond the probe traces, a training method, or an operating threshold. We should not present any of those choices as part of the specified run.
Could we report accuracy instead of AUROC?

Accuracy could be a different measure, but it would not replace the activity's stated jam-offset AUROC score. AUROC assesses discrimination across thresholds; accuracy depends on a particular way of making discrete decisions. The specified measure here is AUROC.
What does scoring peak force add if AUROC is high?

It keeps the force outcome visible independently of discrimination. Even if the traces distinguish jams from offsets well, that fact alone says nothing about the highest force observed during probing. OccludedProbe-0.2 calls for both scores, without assuming that one implies the other.
Should peak force be described as the force for a complete insertion trial?

Not on the basis of this activity. It calls for peak-force scoring in the occluded-probe evaluation. It does not say that complete insertion trials, including every possible recovery action, are being evaluated here.
So a peak-force result from this run would not, by itself, prove the broader below-20 N trial requirement?

Correct. The broader requirement concerns peak contact force below 20 N in at least 99% of trials, including jam recovery. Scoring peak force for OccludedProbe-0.2 is relevant, but this activity alone does not state that full insertion trials are assessed or that the broader requirement is met.
Does running probes capped at 18 N automatically mean every scored peak is below 18 N?

No measured peaks are given. The 18 N cap specifies how the probes are intended to be constrained; the peak-force score assesses what occurs. We should not infer an observed force distribution or a guarantee for all collected cases from the cap alone.
Does the name of the run imply we've already completed data collection?
No. “Run OccludedProbe-0.2” is the activity to carry out. Collection, labeling, and scoring are its stated components, not completed steps or reported findings.
How should we describe its scope without promising full insertion performance?

Describe it as an occluded-probe evaluation on held-out geometries and frictions: collect labeled 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped probe wrench traces and score jam-offset AUROC and peak force. It assesses the probe-based distinction and observed probing forces; it does not itself establish an insertion-success rate.
Give me the activity statement in a single line.
Run OccludedProbe-0.2: collect labeled wrench traces from occluded 0.1 mm, 18 N-capped probes, and score jam-offset AUROC and peak force on held-out geometries and friction conditions.
What did OccludedProbe-0.2 show on the held-out conditions?

On held-out geometries and friction conditions, jam-offset AUROC reached 0.93. Also, 99.3% of probes stayed below 20 N. Those are the reported discrimination and force observations for OccludedProbe-0.2.
Is the 0.93 figure an insertion-success rate?
No. It is jam-offset AUROC: a measure of how well scores distinguish labeled jams from labeled offsets across decision thresholds. It does not report how many complete insertions succeeded.
Can I say the probe classified 93% of cases correctly?
No. AUROC of 0.93 is not 93% classification accuracy at a chosen threshold. The evidence gives no operating threshold or corresponding count of correct individual classifications.
What is important about the geometry and friction conditions being held out?

It locates the reported AUROC on geometries and friction conditions held out from development, rather than only on familiar conditions. The evidence does not list the conditions or give a separate AUROC for each geometry, friction condition, or pairing.
Does 0.93 mean every held-out condition was easy to distinguish?
No. A reported AUROC across held-out conditions does not, on its own, establish uniform performance in every condition. No condition-by-condition results are supplied.
Remind me what the force percentage actually says.
It says 99.3% of probes stayed below 20 N. The unit of that statement is probes, and “below” excludes a peak of exactly 20 N. It is not a statement that every probe stayed below 20 N.
Can we infer what happened on the other probes?

Only to the extent implied by the percentage: the remainder did not fall in the reported below-20 N group. The evidence does not give their peak forces, say whether any were exactly 20 N, or explain their contact conditions.
These were described as 18 N-capped probes. Why report a below-20 N observation instead of saying they all stayed below 18 N?

The 18 N cap describes the probes used in OccludedProbe-0.2; the reported observation is specifically that 99.3% of probes stayed below 20 N. That observation cannot be rewritten as a claim that every observed peak was below 18 N. The evidence does not provide the distribution of measured peaks relative to 18 N.
Does the force figure include full jam-recovery trials?

The reported percentage is for probes. It does not say that complete insertion trials or jam-recovery sequences were included in that percentage. We should keep probe-level force observations distinct from trial-level force outcomes.
Do we know whether the probes that weren't below 20 N were jams or offsets?
No. The evidence gives an overall probe percentage, not a force breakdown by jam-versus-offset label. It does not identify which labeled cases accounted for the remaining probes.
